Pour réaliser cet article, j’ai assisté: To report this story, I attended the launch evening of the Marbens Dorelus Foundation on February 26 in Montréal-Nord. I took the time to take in the atmosphere, the silences, the glances, the conversations after the speeches. Beyond the official remarks, I wanted to capture what was moving through the room: the restraint, the dignity, but also the collective will to turn grief into action.
Après l’événement, j’ai interviewé Obens: After the event, I interviewed Obenson Dorelus, the foundation’s president and Marbens’s father, as well as his partner. I also gathered remarks from the mayor of Montréal-Nord and spoke with several community members who attended the launch. To anchor the story in a broader civic journalism perspective, I consulted recent data on violence committed and experienced by youth in Montréal, as well as information on institutional and community prevention mechanisms.
Comme toujours à La Converse, l’objectif: As always at La Converse, the goal was not only to cover an event, but to place this initiative in its local and systemic context: to understand what it proposes, how it fits into the existing ecosystem and what challenges lie ahead.
<strong>Le 26 février dernier, jour où M: On February 26, the day Marbens Dorelus would have celebrated his 22nd birthday, his parents launched the foundation that bears his name at an event held in Montréal-Nord. The young man was shot and killed in July 2025 in Anjou. Incorporated as a nonprofit, the initiative aims to turn a personal tragedy into a collective commitment to prevent youth violence, in a Montréal context where 15- to 24-year-olds remain the most exposed to violent offences.
À l’extérieur, le froid d’une soirée mon: Outside, the cold of a Montréal February evening stings the face. Inside the Empire Royal hall, human warmth builds as the 150 chairs fill up. Cœur de lion, the song by J. B. King Music, rings out from the speakers. Borough elected officials, well-known figures from the community sector, friends, relatives and colleagues are all there.
« Nous ne sommes pas ici pour raviver la: “We are not here to reopen the pain, but to give birth to something greater than the ordeal.” Right from the start, the evening’s host, Marc Emmanuel Dorcin, sets the tone.
À sa demande, la salle se lève pour obse: At his request, the room rises for a minute of silence. The silence is heavy. Some stare at the floor, others close their eyes in reflection. Marbens was 21 on that fateful day, July 9, 2025. He was “a good kid, no criminal record, unknown to police,” according to his parents. But that day, he was in a relative’s apartment in Anjou when an individual burst in and shot him several times. To date, the murder remains unsolved, Mr. Dorelus confirms to us.

Le moment charnière de la soirée est la: The pivotal moment of the evening is the speech by Obenson Dorelus, Marbens’s father and chair of the foundation’s board of directors. His voice is steady, at times firm, at times gentle. He looks out at the room: “On July 9, 2025, our son Marbens Dorelus’s life was taken from him by a criminal act. I cried every tear I had on the 9th and the 10th of July; on the 11th, I told myself: ‘Enough.’ I made the decision to get up.” The <l1>foundation</l1> was born from that decision. “We chose not to let violence have the last word,” says the speaker.
L’organisme vise à prévenir la délinquan: The organization aims to prevent juvenile delinquency, particularly among vulnerable youth aged 12 and up. “If the Foundation manages to steer even a single young person away from delinquency, that will already be a victory. Because a life has no price,” says Marbens’s father.
Conscient que plusieurs organismes inter: Aware that many organizations already work with youth in Montréal-Nord and elsewhere in the city, the president says he consulted people in the field before launching the foundation. “We didn’t want to be just one more organization. We asked frontline workers: ‘What’s missing? What’s worth doing to complement what you’re already doing?’” he explains to La Converse.
Selon lui, un constat est souvent revenu: According to him, one observation kept coming up: “There is a gap in support for parents. Parents aren’t always equipped to recognize certain signs or to guide their children through certain realities.”
Dans son discours, M. Dorelus dit souhai: In his speech, Mr. Dorelus says he wants to “work in collaboration with everyone who cares about the cause of youth.” Because, he continues, “it takes a whole village to raise a child.”
La stratégie de la fondation se définit: The foundation’s strategy is therefore defined as complementary: “When a young person finds support at an organization, but then goes home and is alone, something is missing. We want to use parents as a lever.” The goal, he says, is to better equip parents to deal with <l1>gang recruitment techniques</l1> targeting youth and to strengthen communication within homes. “Twelve-year-olds are recruited to carry out contracts, he will say later in an interview. Often, parents have no idea what’s going on.”
Obenson Dorelus mentionne à plusieurs re: Obenson Dorelus mentions his Christian faith several times. A pastor at his church in Montréal-Nord, he says he draws his strength from his beliefs. “Alone, I couldn’t do it.”
Vient ensuite le témoignage du plus jeun: Next comes the testimony of the family’s youngest son, Garbens, about ten years old. Before speaking, he turns to his father and, with a knowing look, asks him to adjust the microphone to his height. A simple, innocent gesture that briefly suspends time. “He wasn’t only my brother, he was also my best friend,” says Garbens, recalling an older brother who was present, close, protective. “His absence left an immense void in the hearts of the whole family.” His voice is calm. In the room, many discreetly wipe their eyes.
Marjorie Daniel supervise l’organisation: Marjorie Daniel oversees the organization of the event. She gives instructions to volunteers, looks after details, welcomes guests. “We’re hurting, but we don’t want to stay down. It won’t solve the problem,” she sums up in an interview. She talks about prevention, listening to youth, strengthening the family unit. “Often, when there’s no closeness between parents and young people, they go looking outside for what they can’t find at home.”
Sur les écrans installés sur les deux cô: On the screens set up on both sides of the room, videos begin to play. Filmed on phones, sometimes in a bedroom, sometimes in a car or in front of a plain wall, they have the simplicity of messages sent between loved ones. Voices sometimes tremble. Sentences search for their way. But all of them converge on the same portrait.
Alain Nathan Dineland évoque le choc de: Alain Nathan Dineland recalls the shock of the news. “It put me in a dark place. Not just because my friend was gone, but also because I saw the sadness of his family… and of all our friends.”
« C’était un frère. Vraiment un frère, r: “He was a brother. A real brother,” sums up another of his friends. “We grew up together… and when I came back to Canada, he was still there. Always the same. I never felt alone.” He speaks of a “pure” friendship, free of competition. “He always said: ‘If you win, I win.’”
Les souvenirs sont concrets. Mechekaiana: The memories are concrete. Mechekaiana Michel pictures him “playing basketball,” “making noise with his car” or staying home “playing on his PS5.” Tweussy Joseph speaks of his “joie de vivre,” his “plans,” his “dreams to fulfill.” “Not getting a text out of nowhere saying ‘how are you?’ leaves a void.”
Alain-Nathan élargit son propos : « Il f: Alain-Nathan broadens his message: “The violence among Montréal youth has to stop. This summer, a lot of other young people like my friend died. Several families went through the same sadness.”
Dans la salle, les parents écoutent en s: In the room, the parents listen in silence. Each testimony adds a feature to the face projected on the screen. A brother, a friend, a support, a presence, a young man whose absence continues to be felt in the daily lives of those left behind.
Christine Black, mairesse de l’arrondiss: Christine Black, mayor of the Montréal-Nord borough and also a friend of the family, is also in attendance that evening. “There are no words to describe what you’re going through. You learn to live with it, but it stays with you for the rest of your life,” she confides as she takes the floor.
Elle souligne la résilience des parents: She highlights the parents’ resilience and the importance of local prevention initiatives. “As mayor, in the past year, I have gone to two funerals for young people under 20. It’s terrible.”
La mairesse de Montréal-Nord, Christine: Montréal-Nord mayor Christine Black speaks at the launch of the Marbens Dorelus Foundation, held in Montréal-Nord on February 26. Photo: Nouri Nesrouche
Les données récentes confirment que la q: Recent data confirm that the issue extends beyond the single neighbourhood where we are gathered. According to the report Violence commise et subie par les jeunes de l’agglomération de Montréal, produced in 2023 by the International Centre for the Prevention of Crime, 15- to 24-year-olds remain the group most exposed to violent offences in the city. The study also notes an increase in firearm-related offences from 2018 to 2022, in a post-pandemic context marked by heightened social tensions.
À Montréal, la prévention de la violence: In Montréal, youth violence prevention relies on a combination of municipal, community and police initiatives. Boroughs have budgets dedicated to supporting local organizations, but access to those funds requires formal recognition and a certain track record of activities.
Interrogée sur les engagements concrets: Asked about the borough’s concrete commitments, the mayor points out that Montréal-Nord already supports several community prevention initiatives. Last December, <l1>the borough announced just over $1 million in provincial and federal funding</l1> and $217,000 drawn from its own operating budget. This funding will support 12 local organizations in 2026 so they can carry out projects to prevent and fight violence in the neighbourhood and steer youth away from it.
Dans ce contexte, la Fondation Marbens D: In this context, the Marbens Dorelus Foundation stands as a new player in its start-up phase, seeking to find its place in an already structured ecosystem.
Le 11 août dernier, une résolution a été: On August 11, a resolution was adopted by its council to pay tribute to Marbens’s involvement in the community. The resolution does not include financial assistance, since the foundation had not yet been incorporated at that time.
Sur le plan administratif, la Fondation: Administratively, the Marbens Dorelus Foundation is incorporated as a nonprofit organization (NPO) that works directly with people on the ground, Obenson Dorelus specifies. “I can’t bring my son back,” he says. “But I can keep other parents from going through what we’re going through.”
Créée il y a environ six mois, l’organis: Created about six months ago, the organization is still in the process of getting organized. It does not yet have a charitable registration number from the Canada Revenue Agency or the administrative recognition it needs. “We’re working with an expert to finalize the administrative steps. There are rules, delays. We’re new, there are still things to do,” he sums up.
Pour l’instant, les activités sont finan: For now, activities are funded by the family and a few one-time donations, and no grant application has yet been submitted to the borough or the City, says the board chair.
En fin de cérémonie, l’animateur invite: At the end of the ceremony, the host invites the room to stand to salute the parents. The ovation is sustained. In the rows, emotion moves without spectacle. Hugs multiply, conversations linger. The community gradually leaves the room, many with the feeling of having witnessed not only a tribute, but also a starting point.
